sources.headline: Haley Stevens backs Mike Rogers. And, Gulf states brace for potential attack on Iran
sources.text:
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories Democratic Rep. Haley Stevens stunned the political landscape by endorsing GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers for Michigan's open Senate seat, breaking with her party less than 48 hours before Election Day. The surprise defection followed weeks of deteriorating relations with her former primary opponent, Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed. In her endorsement of Rogers, Stevens cited El-Sayed's ties to political streamer Hasan Piker, whose remarks concerning Jewish people and Israel sparked backlash in August. El-Sayed sought to distance himself from the controversy, but Stevens has criticized him for not doing enough to reassure Black and Jewish voters who backed her in the primary.
Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers, right, and Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., attend a service at Perfecting Church, Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026, in Detroit.
Jose Juarez/AP
hide caption
Jose Juarez/AP
🎧 NPR's Sam Gringlas tells Up First that he has met Democrats who didn't support El-Sayed in the primary and are struggling with their votes this fall. The latest drama may not sway late deciders, but it's not the discussion the El-Sayed campaign wanted. Many Democrats are angry and now rallying behind El-Sayed. Stevens' longtime chief of staff and many other staff members have quit, and the Michigan Democratic Party chair announced that Stevens is no longer a member. This turmoil exposes deepening fault lines within the party, not just over Israel but also regarding its future identity, Gringlas says. Even if Democrats reclaim one or both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, questions about the party's future are expected to linger, especially as they prepare to choose a presidential nominee in 2028.🎧 Voters are unhappy, NPR's Tamara Keith says, which has shifted a favorable election landscape for Republicans into a challenging position for President Trump and his party. Democrats are urging voters to give them a chance to drive change. Meanwhile, the GOP — as summed up by House Speaker Mike Johnson — has framed the midterms as a "contrast election between common sense and crazy." Keith says midterms typically serve as a referendum on the sitting president and his party, rather than a contrast.➡️ Here are six things to watch for on election night to see who will end up controlling Congress. NPR has a guide on when polls close and where to watch the results come in.➡️ Ahead of Election Day, NPR political correspondents answer listeners' biggest questions about the midterms' potential outcomes and what it's like to cover the excitement of politics.➡️ In every election, a key group of voters influences which candidates prevail. NPR's Politics team shares five insights from a year of engaging with voters who supported former President Joe Biden in 2020 and then switched to Trump in 2024.➡️ The NPR App has all of NPR's election coverage in one place — from the biggest stories across the country to the issues that matter close to home. Browse headlines, playlists, podcast episodes, videos and more, all on the 2026 Election tab.
After tomorrow's elections, Trump may choose to bomb Iran again — an option he has discussed with Israel. The U.S.' partners in the Gulf are on edge and bracing for potential conflict. Qatar has been actively leading negotiations with Iran over the past 72 hours to prevent further fighting. 🎧 Qatar has been tight-lipped about the negotiations, but Iran says there's a two-day plan to stop attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks with the U.S., depending on the U.S. response. Trump said that the U.S. has neutralized key components of Iran's military but has a couple of targets left, according to NPR's Aya Batrawy. Gulf states worry that further attacks will destabilize the region and disrupt global energy supplies. The Supreme Court will hear arguments tomorrow in a case between the Catholic Church and Colorado's taxpayer-funded pre-K programs. The case questions whether religious schools can refuse admission to children of gay and trans parents, which would violate a state law against discrimination. For decades, the Supreme Court upheld the separation of church and state. But in the past 10 years, the court's conservative majority has increasingly shifted focus to the First Amendment's protection of religious freedom. This shift complicates Colorado's inclusive pre-K initiative aimed at ensuring that virtually all 4-year-olds in the state get a pre-K education. To meet its goal, the state included religious schools in its program, as long as they comply with state laws prohibiting discrimination on the basis of race, religion, sexual orientation or gender identity.
Your turn
Getty Images
Getty Images
hide caption
Getty Images
"Your Turn" is a special series from NPR's Allison Aubrey, exploring how to navigate your way through midlife. Burnout can be a challenge during midlife. As work and home obligations take up more of your focus, burnout can slowly sap your sense of joy and wonder in everyday life. Psychiatrist Judith Joseph says there's a term for this: anhedonia. It's the inability or reduced capacity to experience pleasure from things that are normally enjoyable. Joseph says it can accompany what she calls "high-functioning depression," and she describes it as depression's "silent sister." Here's what the research shows about high-functioning depression: ➡️ Research published in the journal Cureus confirmed the hypothesis that people with high-functioning depression have increased levels of anhedonia and trauma. Parents and caregivers had the highest high-functioning depression scores.➡️ High-functioning depression is not an official diagnosis in the DSM-5. People who keep functioning may not recognize their symptoms or seek treatment until they're burned out.➡️ Joseph has developed an anhedonia quiz. While it's not a diagnostic tool, it can be helpful to take stock of the obstacles preventing you from living a more joyful life.➡️ Joseph also developed a framework to combat anhedonia, called the Five V's: Validation, Venting, Values, Vision and Vitals. Want to know more? Read more about the Five V's, sign up for the Your Turn newsletter and listen to the Your Turn podcast for tools and inspiring stories that blend science and wisdom to help you move forward to what's next. Behind the story by Tamara Keith, senior political correspondent
People arrive at a polling location during early voting in the midterm election, in Atlanta, Georgia, on October 13, 2026.
Photo by Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Photo by Erik S. Lesser/AFP via Getty Images
At this stage in the midterms, all that's left is the voting and the waiting. On election night, I'll be in Studio 31 at NPR headquarters with browser tabs full of spreadsheets, watching the results roll in and sharing context with NPR listeners. One of those spreadsheets lists all the congressional districts that have been redrawn since 2024 as part of a mid-decade redistricting push by President Trump. Facing down the historical precedent that the president's party usually loses seats in the midterms, the president pressured Republican-led states to create more sure-thing GOP districts.
But headed into voting, the results in two-thirds of those districts are very much up in the air. In some cases, Democrats are favored. These are places Trump would have won by 10 points just two years ago. Last month, I saw that the president had a campaign rally scheduled in Greenville, N.C. But national Republicans essentially stopped running ads for Michael Whatley — Trump's handpicked nominee — and diverted resources to states with more competitive races. So, why was the president holding another rally? I reached out to a few sources in the state. What I learned is that the real reason for the president's trip was almost certainly to help the Republican candidate in eastern North Carolina's first congressional district. It is now one of the most hotly contested and expensive House races in the country, despite new district lines that should have made it an easy Republican pick-up. Two days of driving through this very large district, one Trump rally, two bags of gummy candy and a lot of coffee later, I was back in the office digging into my spreadsheet of congressional districts. NC-01 isn't an isolated case. A majority of districts redrawn to be a firewall for a Republican majority have turned out to be far more competitive than expected. So, Tuesday night (and beyond), I'll be filling in the wins and losses to see how this gambit turned out. In the meantime, read more from me about how Trump is spending his final days on the campaign trail. And, you can listen to everything you need to know about the midterms on Up First: The Sunday Story. 3 things to know

sources.headline: Democrat endorses Republican candidate in key Michigan Senate race as party spat escalates
sources.text: A Democrat in Michigan has endorsed the Republican candidate in the state's crucial US Senate contest, as a spat with her own party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed escalated just days before the vote.Haley Stevens, a sitting congresswoman who lost out on the Democratic Senate nomination to El-Sayed, made a surprise appearance alongside the Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday."I don't belong in Abdul's campaign," she said in a video posted to X shortly after that appearance. "Who we are as Michiganders is not hate and is not what we are getting out from our Democratic nominee right now.""That's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers," Stevens said.The move stunned many of Stevens' fellow Democrats who condemned her decision to break from the party and switch her support just two days before the election, with one calling it a "despicable betrayal". The public feud between Stevens, a centrist Democrat, and El-Sayed, who represents the party's left-wing, has boiled over in recent days. Stevens called on El-Sayed to denounce a campaign advert from an outside liberal group that linked US support for Israel with high prices. El-Sayed criticised the advert and said he had nothing to do with its contents.Stevens had been scheduled to appear at an event with El-Sayed on Sunday in an effort to display party unity, but he reportedly asked her not to come and she chose to attend a church service with his Republican opponent instead."This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made clear that I was not welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me there," Stevens told reporters as she stood alongside Rogers outside the church.When asked about Stevens' endorsement, El-Sayed told reporters he was focused on the problems Michiganders are facing."At the end of the day, I don't think about Haley Stevens," he said on Sunday. "None of this matters."In downtown Detroit, several Democrats the BBC spoke to said they were disappointed by Stevens' endorsement of Rogers."I just genuinely don't understand it," said Summer Lawrence, a 21-year-old student. "I do think it's a betrayal of the party because the things she stands for are not the same things that he stands for as a Republican.""Maybe she had frustrations with the party," Matthew Barera, another Michigan voter, said.Others, including Republicans who support Rogers, said they doubted it would make a difference to the race."People can see right through her actions, you know? She's just angry," Marissa Lee, a Rogers supporter, told the BBC. "She is not going to make anybody change their mind."Over the weekend, as Stevens' criticism of El-Sayed escalated, a number of Democratic politicians in Michigan publicly encouraged her to end the feud and back the party's candidates more directly.The primary, and the conflict between the pair, has underlined divisions over the party's direction ahead of the 2028 presidential election.Former public health official El-Sayed, who is the son of Egyptian immigrants, has channelled grassroots frustration with Washington politics as well as US ties to Israel.Stevens is a more centrist Democrat - and had the support of party figures such as Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer during the primary race. The party is hoping to regain control of the Senate in Tuesday's elections, but will need a net gain of four seats to do so. A loss in Michigan - which they currently hold - would represent a major blow and leave them needing to flip five seats.

sources.headline: Democrat Haley Stevens endorses Abdul El-Sayed’s Republican rival Mike Rogers
sources.text: Congresswoman Haley Stevens, who lost the Michigan Democratic Senate primary to Abdul El-Sayed, endorsed his Republican rival, Mike Rogers, in an extraordinary rebuke of her party’s nominee on the eve of the midterm elections.Her endorsement came in a video posted to X after she attended an event with Rogers at the predominantly Black Perfecting church in Detroit on Sunday. Stevens’ endorsement was the culmination of an escalating feud between the former primary rivals – primarily over support for Israel – that has roiled one of the most fiercely contested Senate contests of the cycle.Why did a Democrat endorse a rival Republican in Michigan? - The LatestThe endorsement was met with immediate pushback from Democrats, who condemned Stevens for her “betrayal”.Michigan’s Democratic party chair Curtis Hertel said: “Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers – a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump’s agenda – shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about. We reject the attempts by Stevens and bad-faith actors to divide our party and undermine our momentum, and will not allow these 11th-hour distractions deter us.”Haley Stevens snubs fellow Democrat Abdul El-Sayed to back GOP Mike Rogers in Michigan – videoSome of the people who worked for Stevens’ campaign also reportedly quit following her Rogers endorsement. Her longtime chief of staff, Justin German, and her communications director, Logan Basch, were among those who left, according to the CNN correspondent Manu Raju.German later released a statement on behalf of Stevens’ campaign team endorsing El-Sayed: “As Haley Stevens’ Chief of staff for eight years, I speak on behalf of our team in wholeheartedly supporting Abdul El-Sayed for Senate. This election is too important to sow division or stand on the sidelines. We are shocked and heartbroken by Congresswoman Stevens’ decision to support Mike Rogers.”Fallout over Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers continued on Sunday, with figures from the progressive left stepping up to back El-Sayed.Bernie Sanders joined the controversy, attacking Stevens for what Democrats view as an extraordinary betrayal after Stevens accepted El-Sayed’s narrow victory over her in Michigan’s Democrat Senate primaries.“Rep. Haley Stevens’ staff is right to resign in disgust,” Sanders posted on X. “They understand that the election in Michigan is far more important than Haley’s fragile ego and that all of us must stand together to elect Abdul, defeat Rogers and end the Republican rubber-stamp control of the Senate.”Zohran Mamdani, the New York City mayor, said Stevens had “betrayed” working-class people “by endorsing the very Republican she said she wanted to run against”.In his first public comments since Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers, El-Sayed told reporters at a press conference outside a rally he held on Sunday, the very same rally that Stevens had earlier been disinvited from attending, “At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens.” He added, “I’m just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.“If you are somebody who believes that we should stand up to hate, and you have watched this last campaign, I think we probably would not want to support Mike Rogers and Donald Trump and JD Vance,” he said.But Stevens’ political pivot earned her praise from Donald Trump, someone whose policies she has an entire page on her website dedicated to denouncing.Trump, during his rally in Iowa, heaped praise on Stevens for turning against El-Sayed, urging her to join the GOP. “It was an incredible thing,” Trump said. “I’d love her to join the Republican party. I think that could happen.”skip past newsletter promotionafter newsletter promotionStevens had lost by a close margin in this year’s primary, and for months had refused to openly campaign for El-Sayed, unlike his other primary opponent Mallory McMorrow. But top Democrats had brokered the truce between El-Sayed and Stevens. After the two had sparred viciously in the primary campaign Stevens extended him a tepid endorsement, and this weekend was scheduled to join El-Sayed at a predominantly Black church in Detroit’s North End.Those plans have quickly unraveled over an issue that divided Stevens and El-Sayed perhaps more than any other: Israel.Later last week, Stevens, a staunch supporter of Israel, made clear that her appearance alongside El-Sayed was preconditioned on his denouncing an outside group’s campaign ad that had blamed US support of Israel for the rising cost of living. El-Sayed declined the request, accusing Stevens of needlessly reopening debates from a settled primary.As the vicious political firestorm has unfolded, Democratic commentators have also pointed out that Stevens’ fiance, Jason Turkish, has been condemning El-Sayed publicly while supporting Rogers. Turkish, who is also vocally pro-Israel, has donated heavily to Democrats in the past, but this year also donated to Republican candidates including Susan Collins.The California governor, Gavin Newsom, said on the political talkshow 2WAY that Stevens “went another 180 degrees overnight, so something was going on there”.“She’s been successful at taking our eye off the ball and that’s why I understand party leadership condemning it ... This may be curiously the October surprise of sorts,” he added.The Senate majority leader, Chuck Schumer, also responded negatively to the endorsement. Schumer’s campaign account called it a “despicable betrayal” from Stevens in a statement, but continued to push for unity among Democrats.“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors. We Democrats equally united in our total revulsion at the racist, Islamophobic, and over-the-top false attacks on Abdul by Republicans. These attacks are evidence of the total bankruptcy of the Republican Party today, who resort to ugly and un-American fearmongering because they have nothing to offer on the problems that concern people today.”

sources.headline: Michigan Dem Haley Stevens endorses Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers
sources.text: Once-Democratic Senate hopeful, who lost the primary to Abdul El-Sayed, shifts support to his Republican opponent on eve of midterm election.In an unexpected twist, US Representative Haley Stevens, who lost the Democratic Michigan primary for the US Senate to Abdul El-Sayed, has endorsed Republican candidate Mike Rogers.Despite rising tensions between Stevens and El-Sayed in recent days, Stevens shocked party officials on Sunday by throwing her weight behind Rogers. Her endorsement came just two days ahead of Tuesday’s high-stakes US midterm election that will decide which party runs Congress.Recommended Stories list of 4 itemslist 1 of 4What polls say as Trump makes his final push before US midtermslist 2 of 4Where are the most expensive midterm races and who is funding them?list 3 of 4Michigan race: All you need to know about Abdul El-Sayed vs Mike Rogerslist 4 of 4More than 50 million votes cast in US midterm elections: What does it mean?end of list“I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the US Senate. Today, I do not belong to Abdul’s campaign,” she said in a video posted on X after attending a church service with Rogers in Detroit, the state’s largest city.Stevens’s surprise support for US President Donald Trump’s endorsed candidate in the tightly contested race comes after she was uninvited to a joint event on the same day with El-Sayed, who defeated her by a slim margin in the August primary.During an interview on Sunday, the Democratic congresswoman, whose term expires in January, wouldn’t answer whether the rescission of that invitation was what drove her to endorse Rogers.Instead, Stevens said that doing so was “a weight off [her] shoulders”.Long-simmering campaign tensionsThe decision follows months of fraught relations between the two Democrats over Israel, exposing rifts within the party as it fights to win control of Congress.Stevens, who received tens of millions of dollars from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC), has swung between supporting El-Sayed during the campaign and clashing with him over Israel.El-Sayed is an outspoken critic of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza and US military aid to the country.After campaigning for El-Sayed despite their bitter primary fight, Stevens last week openly condemned the candidate for an advertisement that she described as anti-Semitic.The advertisement, by an independent group backing El-Sayed, shows a couple limiting their grocery items because they need to save that money for “killing Palestinians”.El-Sayed said the advertisement was not produced by his campaign and that he disagreed with its message.Stevens told The New York Times on Friday that she had planned to vote for El-Sayed. But she endorsed Rogers two days later, after being uninvited to a church service with El-Sayed in what was intended as a show of Democratic unity.El-Sayed was dismissive of Stevens throwing support behind Rogers, saying he was focused instead on the campaign and voters.Democratic Michigan state Senator Mallory McMorrow, who ran for the US Senate before dropping out ahead of the primaries, told Al Jazeera that Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers will not help Republicans win more votes.“If anything, I think it’s going to backfire,” she said, maintaining that the move angered Michigan voters.Democrats have pledged to act as a check on Trump if they win control of Congress, including blocking funding for the US-Israel war on Iran and the president’s tariffs. Michigan’s Senate race is considered key to that effort.Polls indicate Democrats are likely to win control of the House of Representatives, while the Senate, which Republicans currently lead by a 53-47 majority, is considered a toss-up between the two parties.Michigan is one of a handful of highly competitive Senate races nationwide. Polling suggests El-Sayed is pulling ahead of Rogers – who is supported by Trump and has denied his 2020 election loss – by about five to seven percentage points in the last week.

Michigan Senate race upended as Democrat endorses Republican

Congresswoman Haley Stevens backs Mike Rogers over progressive nominee Abdul El-Sayed, who defeated her in the August primary

Agence France-Presse
Published: 5:00am, 2 Nov 2026Updated: 4:02pm, 2 Nov 2026

A Democratic congresswoman in Michigan broke ranks with her party on Sunday to endorse the Republican candidate in her state’s key US Senate race against left-wing progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed.

In a startling display of party infighting just two days before the November 3 midterm election, Haley Stevens, who lost a bruising primary to El-Sayed in August despite being backed by the Democratic establishment, said she was endorsing Republican Mike Rogers.

“This is a very close election, we all know that, but Abdul made very clear that I was not welcome in his campaign,” she told reporters when announcing her endorsement.

Democrats are seeking to wrest control of both chambers of Congress from President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in Tuesday’s midterms, with the Michigan race a key battleground that could help them flip control of the Senate.

Trump praised Stevens for her “bravery”, posting on his Truth Social platform that “Haley said what few people are willing to say”.

“She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did,” he said.

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a campaign rally on Sunday in Detroit. Photo: AP

Sunday’s statement from Stevens was illustrative of internal divisions within the party, with left-wing candidates often clashing with the Democratic Party’s establishment core on key issues.

El-Sayed, a candidate with a rising national profile, has been a vocal critic of the US alliance with Israel, calling for a halt to arms sales to that country.

On Sunday, El-Sayed said he was unbothered by the Stevens announcement.

“At the end of the day, I actually don’t think about Haley Stevens. I think about the 9,999,998 people who are not those two,” he said, referring to Stevens and Rogers.

“Because you know what, I am just less interested in the politics of it all than I am in the policy of it all.”

Democratic backlash against Stevens was fast and furious.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called her move a “despicable betrayal”, while the chair of the Michigan Democrats’ black caucus said Stevens “revealed herself to be a sellout” who has lost her way.

In a CNN interview on Sunday night, Stevens struggled to explain her decision to endorse Rogers.

“I woke up this morning clear-eyed, fresh and focused on what was in my heart and that’s that,” she said, adding that she still wants Democrats to win control of the Senate.

“It’s just where I was at the end of the night and earlier this morning.”

If elected, El-Sayed would be the first Muslim member of the US Senate.

Trump has often singled him out for abuse on the campaign trail, calling him a “jihadist” and claiming he wants to impose Islamic law on the United States.

Most polls put El-Sayed narrowly ahead of Rogers going into Election Day.

sources.headline: 'Despicable betrayal': Democrat backs GOP candidate in key midterms race
sources.text: The Democrats' messy Michigan Senate campaign has again been marred by friendly fire, with defeated primaries candidate Haley Stevens breaking ranks and endorsing the Republican nominee in Tuesday's midterm elections. Analysts are expecting the Democrats to perform well against Donald Trump's Republican Party in many parts of the United States during this week's votes, which could reshape the Congress.But the Democrats' efforts to retain their Senate seat in Michigan have been disrupted by an internal feud between the party's candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Ms Stevens, his rival in the primaries, which has included allegations of antisemitism, racism and xenophobia.The pair's relationship plumbed new depths at the weekend, when Mr El-Sayed announced Ms Stevens was no longer invited to join him at a church service in Detroit on Sunday, local time.The campaign event was meant to show party unity after months of jibes, but it ended up exposing how deep their rift had become.Mr El-Sayed justified the decision by saying he did not want any "distractions", although that hope crumbled when Ms Stevens turned up at a different church with Republican candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday morning.Later that day, she went a step further and held a joint press conference with Mr Rogers, where she said she was a "proud Democrat"."This is a very close election. We all know that," she said."But Abdul made very clear that I wasn't welcome in his campaign, that he didn't need me there, that he didn't want me and at some point you gotta look at who's standing for the country."The Democrats need to retain all of their current Senate seats and flip four more in order to wrest control of the chamber. Chuck Schumer, the Senate minority leader and one of the most senior Democrats in the country, described Ms Stevens's decision as a "despicable betrayal".In a social media post, Mr Trump praised Ms Stevens: "Haley said what few people are willing to say. She showed great and almost unprecedented loyalty to the Great People of Michigan with what she did."At a rally in Iowa later that day, the president said he hoped the Democrat would join his party.Despite Mr Trump's plummeting approval ratings around the country, the Republicans are hopeful of a strong showing in Michigan.Mr Rogers is considered a moderate candidate, and the party has attempted to style Mr El-Sayed, who is attempting to become the first Muslim elected to the US Senate, as a radical socialist (a label he denies).Mr El-Sayed's combative style has earned him plenty of admiration, particularly from left-wingers who believe Democrats should do more to stand up to Mr Trump, although it has also sparked criticism from opponents and some within his own party.Mr El-Sayed is an outspoken critic of Israel, the US military and financial support for the country.Abdul El-Sayed's supporters believe Democrats should do more to stand up to Donald Trump. (Reuters: Rebecca Cook)Ms Stevens, a four-term congresswoman who gave up her seat to run for the Senate, is widely described as being among the most pro-Israel Democrats on Capitol Hill, and has accused Mr El-Sayed of not denouncing Islamic extremist groups strongly enough.She also has accused Mr El-Sayed of being antisemitic and spreading "hate", which he denies. Mr El-Sayed has argued he has faced racist and Islamophobic attacks from Republicans over the course of the campaign.Several of Ms Stevens's staff reportedly resigned after her decision to back Mr Rogers.Speaking on Sunday, Mr El-Sayed batted away questions about Ms Stevens's decision."I'm not in the business of driving clicks for you. I'm in the business of trying to solve problems for the people of my state," he told reporters."None of this matters. The rest of this is just a distraction."Mr Rogers said he was honoured to have Ms Stevens's support."This is courage in politics in America today," he said.Michigan's diverse population has made political battles in the state increasingly nuanced and complex.Outside a campaign event for Mr El-Sayed, one of his supporters, Roseanne Simons, dismissed Ms Stevens's move."It's not about her. And I would prefer to not even use her name right now. It's about getting the best candidate," she said.Ali Tariq, another supporter, said he did not think the Democrats' campaign had been derailed."I've always kind of seen her as a closet Republican," he said.The state's largest city, Detroit, and its surrounding suburbs host a large Muslim population, a dominant Black community, and a sizeable Jewish contingent.During the 2024 presidential election, former US vice-president Kamala Harris, who was the Democratic nominee, lost critical support within the state's Arab and Muslim communities because they believed the Biden administration was too supportive of Israel.Republicans are also targeting moderate, socially conservative Black voters by bombarding Detroit television stations with commercials portraying the progressive Democratic nominee as dismissive of the city's community interests.
